relearning.title: Read: Newton's 3rd law
relearning.description: A short reading with the dance-partners analogy, worked examples and quick checks.

body.text:
**I can calculate and explain Newton's 3rd Law.**

**Think of dance partners.** Forces always come in pairs, and both partners move at the same time. If one skater pushes another away, both skaters roll apart. You can't push on something without it pushing back on you.

**Newton's 3rd law:** For every action there is an **equal and opposite reaction**. Whenever one object exerts a force on a second object, the second object exerts an equal and opposite force on the first object.

**Find the reaction: switch the two objects and flip the direction.** You push the wall, so the wall pushes you. A rocket pushes gas down, so the gas pushes the rocket up. A swimmer pushes water back, so the water pushes the swimmer forward.

**Worked example:** A student on roller skates pushes a wall with 60 N. Switch and flip: the wall pushes the student with **60 N** in the opposite direction. The forces are equal, even though only the student moves.

checks.prompt: A soccer player's foot pushes the ball forward. What is the reaction force?

options.text: The ground pushes the ball forward
Gravity pulls the ball down
The ball pushes the foot backward

checks.explanation: Switch the two objects and flip the direction: foot on ball, forward, becomes ball on foot, backward. Picking a different force, like gravity on the ball, is the common mistake.

checks.prompt: A student pushes on a parked car with 150 N, and the car doesn't move. How hard does the car push back on the student? Type a number (in N).
checks.explanation: Action and reaction are always equal: the car pushes back with 150 N, in the opposite direction. Thinking the car pushes back less (or not at all) because it doesn't move is the common mistake.

sections.title: Equal forces, different accelerations

body.text:
**Equal forces, different results.** The two forces are always the same size, even in a collision: a heavy and a light football player hit each other with **equal** forces. What is different is the **acceleration**. Use **a = F ÷ m**: the object with less mass gets the bigger acceleration. That's why a skater rolls away from a wall, but the wall doesn't move.

**Why pairs don't cancel.** Action and reaction act on **different objects**, so they never go on the same FBD. The weight (Fg) and normal force (FN) on a book both act on the book, so they are **not** a 3rd-law pair.

**Worked example 2:** Two students, 50 kg and 60 kg, sit on scooter boards and push apart with 120 N each. Formula: a = F ÷ m. Set up: 120 N ÷ 50 kg and 120 N ÷ 60 kg. Answer: **2.4 m/s²** and **2.0 m/s²**. Same force, but the lighter student gets the greater acceleration.

**Momentum in collisions and recoil.** When two objects push on each other, their total momentum (mass × velocity) is the same before and after. If they start at rest and push apart, their momenta are equal and opposite: **m1 × v1 = m2 × v2**.

**Worked example 3:** Two skaters, 40 kg and 50 kg, stand still and push apart. The 40 kg skater moves at 2.5 m/s. Set up: 40 kg × 2.5 m/s = 100 kg·m/s, so v2 = 100 kg·m/s ÷ 50 kg. Answer: **2.0 m/s** the other way.

**Watch out for:** saying the heavier or faster object pushes harder (the forces are always equal), calling weight and normal force a 3rd-law pair, thinking the pair cancels (different objects!), and using the wrong mass when you find each object's acceleration.

checks.prompt: A loaded truck and a small car bump into each other. Which statement is correct?

options.text: They push on each other with equal forces, and the car gets the greater acceleration
The truck pushes harder, so the car gets the greater acceleration
They push with equal forces, so they get equal accelerations

checks.explanation: The 3rd law makes the forces equal. With a = F ÷ m, the smaller mass (the car) gets the greater acceleration. Saying the heavier truck pushes harder is the common mistake.

checks.prompt: A 45 kg student and a 75 kg student push off each other on scooter boards with 90 N. What is the 45 kg student's acceleration? Type a number (in m/s²).
checks.explanation: Each student feels the same 90 N. Use that student's own mass: a = F ÷ m = 90 N ÷ 45 kg = 2 m/s². Using the other student's mass (90 ÷ 75 = 1.2) is the common mistake.

sections.shortAnswer: Explain why the weight of a book and the normal force from the table are NOT an action-reaction pair.

relearning.title: Do: flip the pairs, then work a recoil problem
relearning.description: Action-reaction flashcards with a 3-question self-quiz, then a recoil problem one step at a time.

cards.back: For every action there is an equal and opposite reaction. To find it, switch the two objects and flip the direction.
The wall pushes on you, with the same size force, in the opposite direction.

cards.front: A rocket pushes hot gas down
cards.back: The gas pushes the rocket up.

cards.front: A swimmer's arms push water back
cards.back: The water pushes the swimmer forward.

cards.front: Your feet push the Earth down when you jump

cards.back: The two forces act on different objects, so they never go on the same FBD.
The forces are equal, but a = F ÷ m: the smaller mass gets the bigger acceleration.

checks.prompt: A firehose pushes water out the front. What is the reaction force?

options.text: The water pushes the hose backward
The water pushes the hose forward
Gravity pulls the water down

checks.explanation: Switch and flip: the hose pushes the water forward, so the water pushes the hose backward. That is why firefighters brace. Forgetting to flip the direction is the common mistake.

checks.prompt: Which pair of forces is NOT an action-reaction pair?

options.text: A paddle pushing water back, and the water pushing the paddle forward
A foot pushing the ground back, and the ground pushing the foot forward
A book's weight, and the table's normal force on the book

checks.explanation: A 3rd-law pair acts on two different objects. The book's weight and the normal force both act on the book, so they are balanced forces, not a pair. The other two switch the objects (paddle and water, foot and ground). Calling any equal and opposite forces a pair is the common mistake.

checks.prompt: A skater pushes off a wall and rolls away, but the wall doesn't move. Why?

options.text: The skater pushes harder than the wall pushes back
The wall doesn't push back
The wall has much more mass, so the same force barely accelerates it

checks.explanation: The forces are equal (3rd law). By a = F ÷ m, the wall, attached to the building, has a huge mass and almost no acceleration. Saying the forces are unequal is the common mistake.

body.problem: A 300 kg cannon at rest fires a 5.0 kg ball forward at 90 m/s. How fast does the cannon recoil backward?

steps.text: Before firing, nothing moves, so the total momentum is 0. After firing, the ball and the cannon must have equal and opposite momentum.
Ball's momentum: momentum = m × v = 5.0 kg × 90 m/s = 450 kg·m/s forward.
So the cannon's momentum is 450 kg·m/s backward. To find its speed, divide by its mass: v = momentum ÷ m.
Set up: v = 450 kg·m/s ÷ 300 kg. Answer: 1.5 m/s backward. Same push on both, but the heavy cannon moves much more slowly than the light ball.

checks.prompt: Your turn: a 4.0 kg medicine ball is thrown at 6.0 m/s. What is its momentum? Type a number (in kg·m/s).
checks.explanation: Momentum = m × v = 4.0 kg × 6.0 m/s = 24 kg·m/s. Dividing (0.67) or adding (10) are the common mistakes.

checks.prompt: Two skaters stand still and push apart. The 50 kg skater moves at 3.0 m/s. How fast does the 75 kg skater move the other way?
checks.explanation: Their momenta are equal and opposite: 50 kg × 3.0 m/s = 150 kg·m/s, so v = 150 kg·m/s ÷ 75 kg = 2.0 m/s. Giving both the same speed (3.0) or swapping the masses (4.5) are the common mistakes.

checks.prompt: A student on roller skates pushes a wall with 40 N. What does the wall do?

options.text: Pushes the student with 40 N in the opposite direction
Nothing, because the wall doesn't move
Pushes the student with less than 40 N

checks.explanation: Switch the two objects and flip the direction: the wall pushes the student with an equal 40 N the opposite way. That's why the student rolls back. Thinking the wall can't push because it doesn't move is the common mistake.

checks.prompt: A swimmer pushes the water backward. What is the reaction force?

options.text: The swimmer pushes the water forward
The water pushes the swimmer forward
Gravity pulls the swimmer down

checks.explanation: Switch the objects (swimmer pushes water → water pushes swimmer) and flip the direction (backward → forward). Gravity is a different force, not the reaction. Forgetting to switch the objects is the common mistake.

sections.title: Newton's Laws: Crash Course Physics #5

checks.prompt: A 100 kg football player and a 50 kg player run into each other. What is true about the forces and accelerations?

options.text: The 100 kg player pushes harder
The forces are equal, and the 50 kg player gets the bigger acceleration
The forces are equal, and both players get the same acceleration

checks.explanation: Action and reaction are always equal, even in a collision. Use a = F ÷ m: the player with less mass gets the bigger acceleration. Saying the heavier player pushes harder is the common mistake.

checks.prompt: Two students, 40 kg and 80 kg, sit on scooter boards and push apart with 160 N each. What is the 40 kg student's acceleration? Type a number (in m/s²).
checks.explanation: a = F ÷ m = 160 N ÷ 40 kg = 4 m/s². The 80 kg student gets only 2 m/s² from the same force. Using the wrong student's mass is the common mistake.

sections.shortAnswer: A small car and a big truck collide head-on. Explain which one pushes harder on the other, and which one has the bigger change in motion.
